newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ monetary easing seen soon despite MPS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ monetary easing seen soon despite MPS.

text.p: Economists still see scope for further easing in New Zealand's monetary conditions over time, despite a surprisingly bearish statement from the Reserve Bank on Tuesday.
"They look to be playing a very cautious hand," said Bank of New Zealand Treasury Economist Peter Jolly. "I think the market will continue to discount further easings."
National Bank chief economist Adrian Orr agreed.
"A very cautious statement. They have erred on the side of chasing credibility."

Earlier on Tuesday, the RBNZ's six-monthly monetary policy statement (MPS) surprised financial markets by qualifying its acceptance of a recent market-led easing in monetary conditons with a comment that the market's reaction had been "somewhat excessive".

Interest rates and the currency fell dramatically last week on the back of the formation of a new centre-right National-NZ First coalition government. The market had expected RBNZ governor Don Brash to sanction the easing and were disappointed the endorsement was only partial.
"It seemed to me that there was a bit of hope that Don Brash would come out and say the easing was fine, go for your life," said one dealer.

Brash said the bank needed to be cautious about the extent and speed of any easing, given the fiscal uncertainties under the new government. The bank would have preferred to see conditions move rather more moderately, Brash said.
The currency continued to climb after an initial spike higher on the back of the statement, and dealers said it could well tackle 71 US cents from its 69.85 cent open.
The reaction in the money market was more muted, with 90-day bank bill rates settling back around their 7.90 percent open after slight selling.
National Bank's Orr said while conditions appeared set to remain firm in the very short term, there should be room over the March 1997 quarter to see 90-day bank bill rates fall further.

ANZ Bank economists backed that comment, saying the scope for an easing during the March quarter would be enhanced if December quarter inflation data, due in January, confirmed moderating inflation pressures.

In the meantime, however, the MPS showed the Reserve Bank remained concerned about the fiscal outlook, and was also wary of rising inflation expectations after the target band was widened to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, economists said.
Brash made it clear the bank would not be content with projecting inflation at or close to three percent.

He also expressed concern at the stronger-than-expected import prices in the September quarter and rising monetary and credit aggregates, saying it was possible aggregate inflation would turn out to be higher than the RBNZ had projected.
Bancorp Treasury Services said the MPS sanctioned current levels and revealed the RBNZ's concern about the rapid pace of the recent rally rather than its extent.

Doyle Paterson Brown chief economist Stephen Toplis said the bank was in a period of significant uncertainty as it tried to establish the impact on inflation of various new government policies. However, he saw an easing further down the track.
"The bank, given the part of the economic cycle that we're in, is leaning towards an easing bias over time," Toplis said.
